docs.title: From Digital Edition to Computational Music Analysis
docs.text:
Von der digitalen Edition zur computergestützten Musikanalyse: Einführung in Musik-Encoding und Tools für die Notentextanalyse Seminar, winter semester 2026/27. Materials in English.

This site carries the content of each session together with demos that run in your browser. Every demo also comes as a Jupyter notebook, where you change the inputs and keep your work: in session 1 on Jupyter4NFDI, from session 2 on your own laptop or, without a laptop, in the cloud.

docs.text: Session Demos 1 Why encode music? From notation to machine-readable scores player-piano roll, one melody in seven formats, binary grids, an LLM writes ABC 2 Building an edition: the source and the notes setup on your laptop, a wrong note in Schumann, OMR next to the scan, five notes in ABC, the page and its bars

docs.title: What the course covers
docs.text:
1. Encoding: why music needs to be encoded, and how formats from ABC and kern to MusicXML and MEI differ.
  2. Digital editions: MEI, facsimiles and editions linked to their sources.
  3. Analysis: note tables, piano rolls, statistics and pattern search with CAMAT.

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
• Verovio renders music notation in the browser and in Python.
  • Jupyter4NFDI runs the notebooks in the cloud: in session 1 for everyone, later for anyone without a laptop. See Setup.
  • mei-friend edits MEI files in the browser, from session 3 on.
  • VS Code, Python and Git run the notebooks and keep your edition's history on your laptop from session 2 on: see Setup on your laptop.
  • CAMAT (Computer-Assisted Music Analysis Toolbox) from session 2 on.

docs.title: Setup on your laptop
docs.text:
From session 2 on, we work on your own laptop. You open the notebooks in VS Code, run them with Python, keep the history of your edition with Git, and share it on GitHub. We set this up together in class, step by step.

How to use this page

  • Choose your system in the first tab (Windows, macOS or Linux). All tabs on the page then switch to it.
  • Do the steps in order. Each step ends with a ✓ Check. Only go on when you see what the check describes.
  • If a check fails, open If it goes wrong below it. If that does not help, raise your hand. Many problems are the same for several people, so asking early saves everyone time.
  • You need about 2 GB of free disk space and the password of your laptop (installers ask for it).

Optional: download the installers at home

The university Wi-Fi gets slow when everyone downloads at once. If you can, download the installers for your system before class (links in steps 2, 3 and 5) and keep them in your Downloads folder.

Step What you get What it is for 1 a GitHub account shares your edition; also signs you in to Copilot 2 VS Code the editor for notebooks and MEI files 3 Miniforge installs Python, the language our notebooks are written in 4 the seminar environment Python, Poppler (reads PDF pages) and the seminar's packages 5 Git keeps the history of your edition 6 VS Code connected to GitHub lets VS Code send your work to GitHub, and switches on Copilot 7 the notebooks a final check that everything works together

docs.title: 1. Create a GitHub account
docs.text:
1. Open https://github.com/signup in your browser.
  2. Enter your e-mail address, a password and a username. Your username appears in your edition's web address, so choose something you are happy to show, for example your name.
  3. GitHub sends a code to your e-mail address. Enter it to verify the account.

GitHub may also ask you to turn on two-factor authentication (a second check when you log in, with an app on your phone). You can do that now or later; GitHub tells you the deadline.

✓ Check: you are logged in at https://github.com and see your username in the top right corner.

If it goes wrong
  • No e-mail arrives: look in your spam folder. University addresses sometimes delay mail by several minutes; you can continue with step 2 and come back.
  • The username is taken: add a number or your initials.

docs.text:

  1. Open https://code.visualstudio.com/download and click the big Windows button. This downloads the User Installer.
  2. Open the downloaded file (VSCodeUserSetup-…exe) from your Downloads folder.
  3. Accept the agreement and keep the default options. On the page Select Additional Tasks, leave Add to PATH ticked.
  4. At the end, leave Launch Visual Studio Code ticked and click Finish.
  1. Open https://code.visualstudio.com/download and click the big Mac button. This downloads a .zip file.
  2. Open your Downloads folder and double-click the .zip. It unpacks into Visual Studio Code.
  3. Drag Visual Studio Code into your Applications folder.
  4. Open it from Applications. If macOS asks whether you want to open an app downloaded from the internet, click Open.
  1. Open https://code.visualstudio.com/download.

  2. Ubuntu or Debian: download the .deb file, then run in a terminal:

    sudo apt install ~/Downloads/code_*.deb

    Fedora: download the .rpm file and run sudo dnf install ~/Downloads/code-*.rpm.

  3. Start Visual Studio Code from your applications menu.

Now add the two extensions we need:

  1. In VS Code, click the Extensions icon in the bar on the left (four small squares), or press Ctrl+Shift+X (macOS: Cmd+Shift+X).
  2. Type Python in the search field. Click Install on Python by Microsoft.
  3. Type Jupyter and install Jupyter by Microsoft.

✓ Check: in the Extensions view, both Python and Jupyter show a gear icon instead of an Install button.

If it goes wrong

  • macOS says the app is damaged or cannot be opened: make sure you moved it to Applications first, then right-click it and choose Open.
  • Several extensions are called "Python": take the one by Microsoft with the blue tick.

docs.title: 3. Install Miniforge
docs.text:
Miniforge installs Python, and it can also install programs that are not written in Python. We need one of those: Poppler, which reads PDF pages.

WindowsmacOSLinux
  1. Download the installer: https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge/releases/latest/download/Miniforge3-Windows-x86_64.exe
  2. Open the downloaded file. Click Next, I Agree, choose Just Me, keep the suggested folder, and keep the default ticks on the last page. Click Install, then Finish.
  3. Open the Start menu, type Miniforge Prompt and open it. A black window appears. From now on, all commands go into this window, not into PowerShell or the ordinary Command Prompt.

To paste a command into Miniforge Prompt, right-click in the window or press Ctrl+V. Then press Enter.

  1. Open Terminal: press Cmd+Space, type Terminal and press Enter.

  2. Copy this line, paste it into Terminal with Cmd+V and press Enter. It downloads the right installer for your Mac:

    curl -fsSLO "https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge/releases/latest/download/Miniforge3-$(uname)-$(uname -m).sh"

  3. Start the installer:

    bash Miniforge3-$(uname)-$(uname -m).sh

  4. Press Enter to read the licence, then Space until its end, and type yes. Press Enter to keep the suggested location. When it asks whether to initialise ("conda init"), type yes.

  5. Close Terminal completely (Cmd+Q) and open it again. From now on, all commands go into Terminal.
  1. Open a terminal.

  2. Download and start the installer:

    curl -fsSLO "https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge/releases/latest/download/Miniforge3-$(uname)-$(uname -m).sh"
bash Miniforge3-$(uname)-$(uname -m).sh

  3. Press Enter to read the licence, then Space until its end, and type yes. Press Enter to keep the suggested location. When it asks whether to initialise ("conda init"), type yes.

  4. Close the terminal and open a new one. From now on, all commands go into this terminal.

Type this command and press Enter:

conda --version

✓ Check: it prints conda and a version number, for example conda 25.9.1. On Windows this happens in Miniforge Prompt.

If it goes wrong
  • Windows: "'conda' is not recognized": you are in PowerShell or the ordinary Command Prompt. Open Miniforge Prompt from the Start menu instead.
  • macOS/Linux: "conda: command not found": close the terminal completely and open a new one. If it still fails, run ~/miniforge3/bin/conda init, then close and reopen the terminal.
  • macOS: curl prints nothing and no file appears: check the Wi-Fi, then run the curl line again.

docs.title: 4. Create the seminar environment
docs.text:
An environment is a separate Python installation for one project. Ours is called seminar. Run these commands one at a time, in the same window as in step 3. Wait until each one has finished, that is, until you can type again.

  1. Create the environment with Python and Poppler. This takes a few minutes:

    conda create -y -n seminar python=3.12 poppler

  2. Switch to it:

    conda activate seminar

    The start of the line changes from (base) to (seminar).

  3. Install the seminar's packages: CAMAT, Verovio and their helpers. This downloads about 800 MB and can take 5–15 minutes. You can start step 5 in the meantime.

    pip install "camat[validation,notebooks]==0.2.8" verovio==6.3.0 pypdf==6.10.0

  4. Check that everything is there:

    python --version
pdftoppm -v
python -c "import camat, verovio; print('ready')"

✓ Check: Python 3.12…, a line beginning pdftoppm version, and ready.

If it goes wrong
  • The line still starts with (base): run conda activate seminar again. You need this every time you open a new window.
  • pip install stops with a network or timeout error: run the same pip install line again. Packages that already arrived are not downloaded twice.
  • "No module named camat": the pip install line did not finish. Look for Successfully installed at its end; if it is missing, run it again inside (seminar).

docs.title: 5. Install Git
docs.text:
WindowsmacOSLinux
  1. Open https://git-scm.com/downloads/win and click Click here to download (the 64-bit Git for Windows Setup).
  2. Open the downloaded file. Click Next on every page, with one exception: on the page Choosing the default editor used by Git, pick Use Visual Studio Code as Git's default editor.
  3. Click Install, then Finish.
  4. Wait until the pip install from step 4 has finished. Then close Miniforge Prompt and open it again, so that it finds Git.
  1. If Terminal is still busy with step 4, open a second window with Cmd+N.
  2. Type git --version and press Enter.
  3. If Git is missing, macOS asks to install the command line developer tools. Click Install and accept the licence. This takes 5–15 minutes.

If the terminal is still busy with step 4, open a second one. Then run, for Ubuntu or Debian, sudo apt install git; for Fedora, sudo dnf install git.

Now tell Git who you are, in a window that is not busy. Every change you record carries this name and e-mail address. Use the e-mail address of your GitHub account:

git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.org"
git config --global --list

If you prefer not to show your address, GitHub gives you a private one under Settings → Emails (it ends in @users.noreply.github.com). Use that one instead.

✓ Check: git --version prints git version 2.…, and the last command lists your user.name and user.email.

If it goes wrong
  • Windows: "'git' is not recognized": close Miniforge Prompt and open it again. If that does not help, restart the laptop.
  • A typo in your name or address: run the git config line again with the right value. It replaces the old one.

docs.title: 6. Connect VS Code to GitHub and Copilot
docs.text:
1. In VS Code, click the Accounts icon (a person) at the bottom of the bar on the left.
  2. Choose the entry that offers to sign in with GitHub. Your browser opens; log in to GitHub and click Authorize. Allow the browser to go back to VS Code.
  3. Open the chat with View → Chat. If VS Code asks you to set up Copilot, choose the free plan.

  4. Try it: copy this question into the chat and send it.

    What does <note pname="f" oct="3" dur="4" dots="1"/> mean?

✓ Check: the Accounts icon shows your GitHub username, and the answer mentions F3 and a dotted quarter note.

Copilot sends whatever you type or attach in the chat to GitHub's servers. Do not paste personal data into it.

If it goes wrong
  • The browser does not return to VS Code: go back to VS Code yourself; it usually shows a box where you can paste the code from the browser.
  • Copilot says you have no access: check that you signed in with the same GitHub account as in step 1, then try View → Chat again.

docs.text:
1. In Miniforge Prompt (Windows) or Terminal (macOS, Linux), make a folder for the seminar and download the notebooks into it:

    conda activate seminar
mkdir seminar-work
cd seminar-work
python -c "import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlretrieve('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/egorpol/camat_lectures/main/get_notebooks.py', 'get_notebooks.py')"
python get_notebooks.py

  2. In VS Code: File → Open Folder…, choose seminar-work, and confirm that you trust the folder.

  3. In the file list on the left, open camat_lectures → 02-building-an-edition → 02_pdf_preparation.ipynb.
  4. Click Select Kernel (top right), then Python Environments…, then seminar.
  5. Click into the first grey code cell and press Shift+Enter. Repeat for each cell, until a cell prints CAMAT: 0.2.8. Stop there; the rest of the notebook is for class.

✓ Check: a cell prints CAMAT: 0.2.8 and pypdf: 6.10.0, with no red error. You are ready.

If it goes wrong

If it is still missing, choose Select Another Kernel… → Python Environments… → Enter interpreter path and type C:\Users\<your name>\miniforge3\envs\seminar\python.exe (Windows) or ~/miniforge3/envs/seminar/bin/python (macOS, Linux).
  • VS Code offers to install ipykernel: click Install.
  • "Poppler's pdftoppm is missing": the notebook uses another Python. Select the seminar kernel as in point 4.

If the cell cannot download anything, download the notebooks from the session page (section Notebooks) and upload them with the Upload button (arrow icon) above the file browser.

Files in your home folder (/home/jovyan) are kept when the server stops; everything else is discarded. Installed packages may have to be installed again after a restart: just run the first cell again.

docs.title: 1. Why encode music? From notation to machine-readable scores
docs.text:
Session 1, 15 October 2026 (double session, 2 × 90 minutes).

Every notation is already an encoding. It was made for a particular reader and a particular use, and it writes down some things while leaving others to the reader's knowledge. Computers, and now language models, are readers without that knowledge, so music encoding formats must state explicitly what human readers infer. Formats differ for the same reason historical notations differ: they serve different users and tasks.

How to use this page

The demos on this page run in your browser; nothing needs to be installed. They load Verovio (about 12 MB) the first time you use them. The same demos come as Jupyter notebooks, where you can change the inputs and keep your work: see Notebooks at the end.

What is Verovio?

Verovio is the program that turns an encoding into a score you can see on this page. It engraves music: it reads an encoded score and draws it as notation (an SVG image). It is built around MEI and converts the other formats on the fly: kern, MusicXML, ABC, Plaine & Easie, EsAC, and the chant formats GABC and Volpiano. It is free and open source (LGPL licence), and the RISM Digital Center leads its development.

Verovio is written in C++ and comes in versions for other languages. This page uses the JavaScript version, which runs inside your browser; the notebooks use the Python version (pip install verovio). Both are version 6.3.0, so page and notebooks show the same score. You can also try it in the Verovio editor, and CAMAT, the library we use from session 2, renders scores with it.

Verovio only shows what the encoding says. When a score looks wrong, look at the encoding first, and then at how Verovio reads it: parts 8 and 10 do both.

By the end of the session you can

  1. explain why a score made for human readers is not enough for a computer;
  2. ask three questions of any notation or format: Who reads it? What does it record? What does it leave out?;
  3. tell a scan, a PDF, an encoded score and a facsimile-linked edition apart, and say who can use each;
  4. place key systems on a timeline from mechanical instruments to kern and the Essen folksong collection;
  5. edit a short ABC, kern or MEI text and render it with Verovio;
  6. turn a melody into a 0/1 grid and say what the grid loses;
  7. check an LLM-written melody against what was asked for.

docs.title: 2. Why encode music?
docs.text:
• Notation is a selection made for a reader who knows the conventions: performance practice, tuning, how to realise an ornament, how repeats work.
  • A computer knows none of this. A scanned score is an image. To search, analyse, render or play music, a machine needs symbols with explicit meaning.
  • Written and performed differ. One written sign (a trill, a grace note, a fermata) stands for performed events that look different from what is written. MEI can keep both, for example @dur (written duration) next to @dur.ges (performed duration).
  • Three questions to ask of every system this semester:
    1. Who reads it? A singer, a lutenist, a cataloguer, a machine, a language model.
    2. What does it record? Pitch, duration, physical action, sound, structure, layout, metadata.
    3. What does it leave out, or leave to the reader?

A digital edition (MEI) encodes what a source says. Analysis (kern, note tables, piano rolls) treats notes as data. The same encoding has to serve both, and that is what this course is about.

docs.title: 3. Scores today: scans, PDFs and facsimile-based editions
docs.text:
Where do you meet scores today? In library digitisations (for example the digital collections of the Bayerische Staatsbibliothek), in PDF archives such as IMSLP, in publishers' editions, and in a few encoded editions. Most "digital" music is a picture of a page.

Form What the computer has You can… You cannot… Scan (TIFF, JPEG; often served through a IIIF viewer) pixels zoom, compare sources, cite a page search for a melody, play it, transpose it PDF page images in a container, at most a text layer download, print, share the same as a scan: the notes are still pictures Encoded score (MusicXML, MEI, kern) symbols with meaning render, play, search, analyse see what the source looked like, unless it is linked Facsimile-linked edition (MEI with <facsimile>) symbols and the page images, linked bar by bar all of the above, and check every bar against the source —

Access: who may use a score? That depends on rights: in the EU, a composer's works are free 70 years after the end of the year of their death, but an edition, an arrangement or a lyricist can still be protected, and countries differ.

Showcase: the eu-pd-composers viewer

The eu-pd-composers viewer (data and code on GitHub) applies the EU rule to the 3,369 composers on Wikipedia's List of 20th-century classical composers, with life dates from Wikidata:

  • 777 are public domain in the EU now (they died in 1955 or earlier), 1,870 are not yet, and 722 have no death date on record. 21 more follow on 1 January 2027.
  • 1,254 are matched to their IMSLP category, with links to 29,033 IMSLP work pages; 20,391 of those pages belong to composers who are public domain now.
  • You can filter by instrumentation, style, citizenship, popularity and the year the works become free.

Figures from the published viewer (dump r019, checked on 2026-10-14). The status is a heuristic based on the composer's death year only, not legal advice: it cannot see lyricists, editions, arrangements or posthumous publications. Check the work itself before you copy, perform or publish it.

Try it: whose music becomes free in the EU on 1 January 2027? Does IMSLP have scores of it?

Accessibility: who can use a score? A screen reader cannot read a scan aloud, a scan blurs when enlarged, and it cannot be turned into music Braille or played back. An encoded score can be all of these (music Braille comes up again in part 4).

Facsimile-based editions keep the source and the encoding together. MEI stores the page images in a <facsimile> element: one <surface> per page, one <zone> (a rectangle) per bar. Each bar of the music points to its rectangle:

<facsimile>
  <surface xml:id="surface_aea1770d9c33" n="1">
    <graphic target="https://api.digitale-sammlungen.de/iiif/image/v2/bsb00023199_00013/full/4134,/0/default.jpg"
             width="4134" height="5495"/>
    <zone xml:id="zone_6ff938b3aec349c48e" type="measure" ulx="852" uly="945" lrx="1593" lry="2290"/>
    <!-- one zone for each of the other 14 bars on the page -->
  </surface>
</facsimile>
...
<pb n="1" facs="#surface_aea1770d9c33"/>
<measure n="1" facs="#zone_6ff938b3aec349c48e"> ... </measure>

(Shortened from the file in Demo E below. The coordinates are pixels in the 4,134-pixel-wide version of the scan.) The encoding stays tied to its witness: every bar can be checked against the page, the source's page and system breaks are kept, and the editor's reading sits next to what the source shows. A traditional critical edition replaces the source with a new engraving and moves the differences into a critical report.

This is where the course is going. The tools of CAMAT, which we use from the next sessions on, grew out of encoding volumes of Denkmäler deutscher Tonkunst from the Bayerische Staatsbibliothek's scans: optical music recognition (OMR) page by page, correction in mei-friend, automatic checks, and measure zones that link every bar back to the scan.

docs.title: Demo E: a facsimile-linked page
docs.text:
The first page of Dietrich Buxtehude's Sonata I in F major, Op. I, for violin, viola da gamba and harpsichord, as printed in Denkmäler deutscher Tonkunst, vol. 11 (1903). Left: the Bayerische Staatsbibliothek's scan, with the zones from the MEI file drawn on it. Right: the same MEI file rendered by Verovio, with the page's three systems. Point at a bar on either side to find it on the other; click to compare it close up. Tick Show the bar's MEI to read how the selected bar is encoded.

Look at bar 11. The 1903 print has the violin's C♯ as a sixteenth note; the encoding follows the first edition, printed in Buxtehude's lifetime, and makes it an eighth note, and an <annot> in the MEI file says so. With Show the bar's MEI ticked you can read it in the code: <staff n="1"> is the violin, n="2" the viola da gamba and n="3" the harpsichord's bass line; each <harm> holds a figure of the figured bass; and the <annot> points at the C♯ with plist. The scan stays the witness, and the encoding records where and why it departs from it. (The note calls the first edition "the 1696 print"; sources date Op. I to about 1694 and Op. II to 1696, so treat the year with care.) The full workflow (OMR, correction, checks) comes later in the course.

Source and licence

MEI: the first page (bars 1–15) of buxtehude_op1_01_sonata_f_major_corr.mei from the CAMAT corpus edition DdT 1, vol. 11: Dietrich Buxtehude, Instrumental Works (work in progress, commit 7af4ae8), MIT License; two ties into bar 16 on the next page were removed. Download the MEI file. Scan: Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, bsb00023199, image 13 (copy of the Hochschule für Musik und Theater München, Bibliothek), licensed CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. The page loads the scan from the library's IIIF server when you open it; it is not copied here.

Discussion: Is a facsimile-linked encoding more authentic than a clean modern edition? Authentic to what: the source, the work, the performance?

docs.title: Demo A: Debussy plays Children's Corner
docs.text:
Debussy recorded Children's Corner himself for the Welte-Mignon (roll 2733). Stanford's SUPRA archive scanned the roll; you can see it in Stanford's viewer. SUPRA turned the scan into two MIDI files:

  • raw: every hole becomes an event: 33,508 holes in 4 tracks (bass and treble notes, and two tracks of expression holes that control loudness);
  • expressive: holes merged into notes and the expression holes turned into loudness and pedalling: 6,031 notes.

Compare the two versions over the same seconds. A long note on the roll is punched as a chain of holes: at 5.1 s the C3 is a 0.1-second hole in the raw file but a 3-second note in the expressive file. The expressive file joins such chains: the 28,365 holes in the raw file's two note tracks become 6,031 notes.

Is a roll a score, a recording or a program? Where are the bar lines and the quarter notes? What is a "note" when 33,508 holes become 6,031 notes?

docs.title: 9. Binary notation: holes, grids and what survives
docs.text:
The roll in Demo A is binary too: there is a hole at a position, or there is not. But a roll is an instruction for a machine: its time runs on continuously along the paper, and a long note is punched as a chain of holes. The grid below is something else: an array that a program computes from a list of notes, with one row per pitch and one column per time step (1 = the pitch sounds). CAMAT builds this kind of grid later in the course to search for patterns. Which bars of Alle meine Entchen can you no longer tell apart?

  • Bars 2 (two half notes), 3 (four quarter notes) and 4 (one whole note) all become a run of four cells. Pure occupancy loses where one note ends and the next begins.
  • Filling the grid needs a rule. The demo has two, under Rules. This demo's rule asks what sounds at the start of each cell: a note shorter than a cell can fall between two cell starts and disappear, and an eighth note on the beat grows to a quarter. CAMAT's rule asks what sounds at any time in the cell: no note is lost, but every note grows to fill whole cells, so on a quarter-note grid two eighth notes in one cell sound together, as a chord. Add eighth notes to the melody and switch the rules. Finer grids keep more but cost size; CAMAT's default cell is a sixteenth note.
  • Reading the grid back needs a rule too. Both rule sets read a run of 1s in one row as one held note, so 1111 comes back as a whole note in bars 2, 3 and 4 alike. The opposite rule, "every 1 starts a new note", would give only quarter notes: bar 3 right, bars 2 and 4 wrong. Without onsets, no rule gets all three right. This demo reads the grid column by column, as a sequence of chords, which works for one melodic line but cuts a note that is held while another pitch moves. CAMAT reads each row on its own. Click the C4 cells in the rest of bar 1 to hold the C under D, E and F, then switch the rules.
  • What would keep the note boundaries? A second grid that marks where notes start ("keep an onset grid", with this demo's rules), or a note table next to the grid, as CAMAT keeps.
  • Two grids are one grid with three values. With the onset grid ticked, each cell is in one of three states: 0 = silence, 1 = a note continues, 2 = a note starts. Two yes/no grids would allow four combinations, but "a note starts where nothing sounds" cannot happen, so three are left: the notation is no longer binary but ternary. Every cell that is not 0 still says "sounding", so a tool written for the 0/1 grid can read the new grid too. CAMAT has no onset layer yet, so the box is greyed out under CAMAT's rules; CAMAT keeps the onsets in its note table.
  • CAMAT does not read its grid back as the music. It slides a small grid, such as a motif, over the grid of a whole piece and scores each position by the cells they share. For every 1 it can keep a pointer to the notes in the score behind it, so a match is shown in the original score, not in a score rebuilt from 0s and 1s. Statistics such as how often each pitch occurs come from its note table, not from the grid. CAMAT's notebooks binary_roundtrip.ipynb and binary_pattern_search.ipynb show both.

docs.title: 10. An LLM writes ABC
docs.text:
ABC is compact text, and there are many tune collections online in it, so language models have seen a lot of it. We ask a model for a melody and check the answer. Because the answer is an encoding, we can test it, which a picture of a score would not allow.

Does every bar add up to the metre? Does Verovio warn? Are the key and the range what was asked for? Is the kern valid at all? Note that the checks rely on how Verovio reads the text: Verovio 6.3, for example, ignores a length written after a chord ([DFA]2), and the page warns when it sees one.

You do not need your own LLM account for this: the recorded answers and the instructor's demo are enough.

docs.title: Addendum: MIDI on a cable and in a file
docs.text:
MIDI comes up in Demo A and in part 7. The name is used for two things: messages sent between instruments, and files that store them.

On a cable: messages, sent as they happen. MIDI 1.0 was published in August 1983 so that instruments from different makers could control each other. A message says what a player does, not what it sounds like: channel 1, key 60 down, velocity 90 is three bytes, 90 3C 5A, and a second message follows when the key is released. The receiving instrument makes the sound; MIDI itself carries no audio. The original cable has five-pin DIN plugs, carries messages in one direction only (from an OUT to an IN socket) at 31,250 bits per second, and has 16 channels, so one cable can play 16 instruments or sounds. A message carries no time: the note starts when the message arrives, and each three-byte message takes about a millisecond on that cable. Today the same messages also travel over USB, Bluetooth and networks, or between programs on one computer.

Here is Alle meine Entchen on the cable, as a sequencer sends it when it plays the file further down. A MIDI monitor, a program that lists the messages coming in, shows each one with the moment it arrived. That time is the monitor's; the cable carries only the bytes.

arrived (s)  bytes      meaning
 0.000       90 3C 5A   key 60 (C4) down, velocity 90
 0.496       90 3C 00   key 60 up
 0.500       90 3E 5A   key 62 (D4) down
 0.996       90 3E 00   key 62 up
 1.000       90 40 5A   key 64 (E4) down
 1.496       90 40 00   key 64 up
 1.500       90 41 5A   key 65 (F4) down
 1.996       90 41 00   key 65 up
 2.000       90 43 5A   key 67 (G4) down
 2.996       90 43 00   key 67 up
 3.000       90 43 5A   key 67 (G4) down
 3.996       90 43 00   key 67 up
 4.000       90 45 5A   key 69 (A4) down
 4.496       90 45 00   key 69 up
 4.500       90 45 5A   key 69 (A4) down
 4.996       90 45 00   key 69 up
 5.000       90 45 5A   key 69 (A4) down
 5.496       90 45 00   key 69 up
 5.500       90 45 5A   key 69 (A4) down
 5.996       90 45 00   key 69 up
 6.000       90 43 5A   key 67 (G4) down
 7.996       90 43 00   key 67 up

That is the whole tune: 22 messages, 66 bytes, eight seconds. Nothing in it says bar, quarter note or tempo. A G lasts one second because its key-up arrives one second after its key-down. A person playing the tune on a keyboard sends the same kinds of messages, at less even times and with a different velocity for each key.

The MIDI specification also has messages it calls real-time messages, in a narrower sense: one-byte messages that keep several machines in step. A sequencer that drives a drum machine sends FA (Start), then F8 (Timing Clock) 24 times per quarter note, at 120 quarter notes a minute one every 21 milliseconds, and FC (Stop) at the end. They carry the beat, but no notes.

In a file: the same messages, each with a wait before it. A Standard MIDI File (.mid) stores the messages and writes before each one how long to wait after the previous one, counted in ticks. The header says how many ticks make a quarter note, and a tempo message says how long a quarter note lasts. Verovio writes the four bars of Alle meine Entchen as a file of 144 bytes. Here is all of it:

4D 54 68 64  00 00 00 06       "MThd": the header, 6 bytes follow
00 01  00 02  00 78            format 1, 2 tracks, 120 ticks per quarter
4D 54 72 6B  00 00 00 0B       "MTrk": track 1, 11 bytes follow
  00     FF 51 03 07 A1 20     wait 0, tempo
  00     FF 2F 00              wait 0, end of track
4D 54 72 6B  00 00 00 67       "MTrk": track 2, 103 bytes follow
  00     FF 58 04 04 02 18 08  wait 0, time signature 4/4
  00     90 3C 5A              wait 0, key 60 (C4) down, velocity 90
  77     90 3C 00              wait 119, key 60 up
  01     90 3E 5A              wait 1, key 62 (D4) down
  77     90 3E 00              wait 119, key 62 up
  01     90 40 5A              wait 1, key 64 (E4) down
  77     90 40 00              wait 119, key 64 up
  01     90 41 5A              wait 1, key 65 (F4) down
  77     90 41 00              wait 119, key 65 up
  01     90 43 5A              wait 1, key 67 (G4) down
  81 6F  90 43 00              wait 239, key 67 up
  01     90 43 5A              wait 1, key 67 (G4) down
  81 6F  90 43 00              wait 239, key 67 up
  01     90 45 5A              wait 1, key 69 (A4) down
  77     90 45 00              wait 119, key 69 up
  01     90 45 5A              wait 1, key 69 (A4) down
  77     90 45 00              wait 119, key 69 up
  01     90 45 5A              wait 1, key 69 (A4) down
  77     90 45 00              wait 119, key 69 up
  01     90 45 5A              wait 1, key 69 (A4) down
  77     90 45 00              wait 119, key 69 up
  01     90 43 5A              wait 1, key 67 (G4) down
  83 5F  90 43 00              wait 479, key 67 up
  00     FF 2F 00              wait 0, end of track

The numbers are hexadecimal: 77 is 119, 3C is 60, and the tempo 07 A1 20 is 500,000 microseconds per quarter note, 120 quarter notes a minute. A wait longer than 127 ticks takes two bytes: 81 6F is 1 × 128 + 111 = 239 (a half note), 83 5F is 3 × 128 + 95 = 479 (a whole note). In 90, the 9 means "key down" and the 0 channel 1. Each key goes up one tick before the next key goes down, so the two Gs of bar 2 are struck twice, not held as one note. The 90 messages are exactly the ones on the cable above; only the waits are new. The FF messages (tempo, time signature, end of track) exist only in files; on a cable, FF alone means Reset. A key "down" at velocity 0 counts as released: the MIDI 1.0 specification allows both this and a separate Note Off message.

On a cable (or USB, Bluetooth) In a file (.mid) What it is a live stream of messages the same messages, stored Time the moment a message arrives a wait in ticks before each message, and a tempo Parts up to 16 channels per cable channels, and tracks played together (format 1) Example a keyboard playing a synthesiser the two files of the Debussy roll in Demo A

The three questions, asked of MIDI.

  • Who reads it? Instruments, sequencers and recording software; SUPRA turned the Debussy roll into MIDI files.
  • What does it record? Which key, how hard (velocity, 0 to 127), when, on which channel, and controllers such as the pedals: the pedal bands in Demo A are Control Change messages 64 (sustain pedal) and 67 (soft pedal).
  • What does it leave out? What a score adds for a reader. C♯ and D♭ are the same key, 61. A note lasts so many ticks; it has no note value, so a short quarter note and an eighth note followed by a rest can look the same. There are no stems, beams, voices, ties, slurs or staff layout.

Why MIDI does not simply turn back into MEI. Turning a score into MIDI is easy: Verovio does it, and there is one right answer. The way back is not. Verovio itself cannot read MIDI (6.3.0 answers "Input format 'midi' is not supported"). A program that imports MIDI into a score has to put back what the score had and the file dropped, and that means guessing. Even for the file above, which a computer wrote from a score, a converter has to decide:

  • Note values. The file says "119 ticks", not "quarter note". Here rounding is easy, because every note is one tick short of a quarter, half or whole note. A person playing the same tune holds the keys for uneven times and drifts in tempo, so a converter must first find the beat and then round each length to a note value (quantisation). Is a short note a staccato quarter, or an eighth followed by a rest? Are three quick notes a triplet or a dotted rhythm? In Demo A's expressive Debussy file, the tempo changes all the time.
  • Metre and bars. The cable carries no bars at all. A file may contain a time signature (Verovio writes FF 58, 4/4) or not. Does the tune start on the first beat, or with an upbeat?
  • Pitch spelling. Key 61 is C♯ or D♭, key 70 A♯ or B♭. The converter has to guess the key and spell each note from it. A file may contain a key signature (FF 59), but it does not have to; Verovio wrote none for this tune.
  • Voices and staves. A piano part is one stream of keys. Which notes belong to the melody and which to the accompaniment? Which go on the upper staff and which on the lower? Where does a voice need a rest?
  • What MIDI never had. Slurs, dynamics (only velocities: 90 for every note here), articulation, beams, layout, and ornaments: a played trill arrives as many short notes. What was not recorded cannot be converted back.

Each of these questions has several possible answers, and different programs answer them differently. Demo C's "Back from the grid to notes" in part 9 is a tiny converter of this kind. It is given the metre, writes every black key as a sharp, chooses the treble or bass clef from the middle pitch, puts all notes into one voice, and needs the onset grid to keep repeated notes apart. MIDI does not need that last help: every note has its own key-down and key-up.

docs.title: 2. Building an edition: the source and the notes
docs.text:
Session 2, 29 October 2026 (double session, 2 × 90 minutes).

In sessions 2 to 4 we build a small digital edition of Robert Schumann's Fröhlicher Landmann, von der Arbeit zurückkehrend (Album für die Jugend, Op. 68 No. 10). An edition is more than an encoding of the notes: it names the source it follows, links every bar to a scan of that source, records what the editor changed and why, and lets others check it. Today we set up our laptops, look at the source, and get the notes in three ways: from a scan, by typing them, and from an existing encoding.

How to use this page

The first block is the setup of your laptop, which we do together with the setup page. If you can, download the installers at home (the setup page says which). No laptop, only a tablet? Then you work in the cloud: choose the tab Cloud in part 1. After the setup, the notebooks of this session are ready: see Notebooks at the end.

By the end of the session you can

  1. open and run the seminar notebooks on your own laptop, or in the cloud;
  2. tell a printed source, its scan, an encoding and an edition apart;
  3. say what optical music recognition (OMR) gives you, and why you still compare it with the scan;
  4. type a few notes in ABC and check them against the print;
  5. find a bar of the print on the page image and in the MEI file.

Today in short

docs.title: 2. Source, scan, encoding, edition
docs.text:
Four things that are easy to confuse:

  • The source. One particular printed edition: Clara Schumann's edition of the Album für die Jugend, Leipzig: Breitkopf & Härtel, plate number R.S. 67 (IMSLP dates it 1887). Editors call a source like this a witness: it is the evidence of what the music says. Other editions of the same piece differ in details.
  • The scan. A photograph of one copy of that print, made by the Bavarian State Library and shared on IMSLP as file 51556: a PDF of 50 pages. No. 10 fills page 8 and has five systems. The print has no bar numbers.
  • The encoding. The notes as text a computer can read. We start from Maja Hartwig's MEI file of this piece in the MEI Sample Collection. It was made from another source, not from our print.
  • The edition. What we make in the next sessions: the encoding, checked against our source, with every bar linked to its place on the scan, our corrections and explanations in the file, and a viewer that shows all this.

docs.title: 3. A wrong note
docs.text:
The melody of this piece is in the left hand. In the first full bar, the print has F, A, C, F: dotted quarter, eighth, dotted quarter, eighth. The MEI file from the Sample Collection has A instead of the last F. The same happens in bar 5, where the melody starts again.

Last bass note of bar 1 and of bar 5 our print (IMSLP 51556, page 8) F3 MEI Sample Collection file A3 our starting file for the seminar F3, corrected

Compare the two files yourself: the same bars from each, with this note in blue. The button Bar 5 shows the second place.

The Sample Collection file also has the tempo words Frisch und munter and the dynamic f. Our starting file leaves them out on purpose (part 7).

Source and licence

Left: Maja Hartwig, Fröhlicher Landmann, MEI 5.1, MEI Sample Collection. The file declares itself public domain; the collection is under the ECL-2.0 licence. The page loads it from GitHub when you open it, and adds the number of staff lines (lines="5"), which the file leaves out: without it, Verovio draws no staff lines. Right: our starting file, made from it for this course: download starter.mei. Its header keeps the credits and says what we changed.

We found this because an OMR program (part 4) read F3 where the file has A3. One look at the scan settled it. So an existing encoding saves a lot of typing, but it does not replace the comparison with your source, note by note. That comparison is the core of editing, and the reason an edition links each bar to the scan.

Pitch names: C4, c′ and kleines c

The notebooks use scientific pitch names: middle C is C4, and the number goes up at each C. In German (Helmholtz) names:

Scientific C3 F3 A3 C4 F4 German c (kleines c) f a c′ (eingestrichenes c) f′

The melody of bar 1 is therefore f, a, c′, f.

docs.title: 4. From a scan to notes: OMR
docs.text:
Optical music recognition (OMR) is a program that looks at the image of a page and proposes notes. It produces a draft, not a transcription: it can miss notes, misread pitches, merge bars, and it usually drops dynamics and words such as Frisch und munter.

Open 02_schumann_omr.ipynb. It shows what two OMR programs, HOMR and OeMeR, made of our page. We ran them before class (each takes minutes), so the notebook only loads the results.

Both are free, open-source research programs. You start them with a command, not in a window with buttons, and both write their result as MusicXML, a common exchange format for scores.

  • HOMR reads photos and scans of printed music. It first finds the staff lines, note heads and bar lines in the image, then reads each staff from left to right with a transformer, the same kind of model that language models use. Its documentation says that it concentrates on pitch and rhythm and leaves out dynamics, articulation and other signs. We used version 0.7.0.
  • OeMeR is the older program on which HOMR's first step is based. It sorts every pixel of the image into staff lines, note heads, stems, clefs, rests and so on, and then builds the music from these pieces, step by step. It is meant to cope with photos taken at an angle. We used version 0.1.8.

Other OMR programs work with a window: Audiveris, also free and open source, shows what it recognised on top of the scan, lets you correct it, and then exports MusicXML. Commercial programs work the same way.

  1. Look at the scan next to HOMR's result for the first two systems.
  2. Compare bar 1 and bar 5 in the bass: which pitch does HOMR read at the end of each bar?
  3. Find one thing HOMR got wrong or left out.
Extension: OeMeR and running OMR yourself

Part 4 of the notebook shows OeMeR on the whole page: it reads most of the right hand in the bass clef, finds 19 bars instead of 21 and loses the C3 of the pickup. Part 5 runs both programs again; that needs extra installations and several minutes per page.

Without installing anything, you can try HOMR on its demo website: upload a picture of a page (JPG or PNG; a screenshot of page 8 of the scan works) and download the MusicXML. Open it in the Any format box in part 5 to see what HOMR read. The website does not say who runs it, so upload only pages you may share, such as our public-domain scan.

docs.title: 5. Typing the notes
docs.text:
The other way to get notes is to type them. Type the bass melody of the pickup and bar 1 in ABC, as in session 1:

  • pickup: C3, eighth
  • bar 1: F3 dotted quarter, A3 eighth, C4 dotted quarter, F3 eighth

The piece is in F major (one flat), in common time, in the bass clef. The box below has the header and the pickup already; type bar 1 after the bar line. Three things you need in ABC:

  • L:1/8 makes the eighth note the unit: G, is an eighth, G,2 a quarter, G,3 a dotted quarter.
  • A comma puts a note one octave lower: C is C4 (middle C), C, is C3.
  • | is a bar line; |] ends the piece.

The score changes as you type. Compare it with the print: pitches and octaves, rhythm, pickup, clef and key. Under the score, Verovio reads lists the notes in words, so you can check them against the list above. The same exercise is part 1 of 02_note_entry.ipynb; you can also download the box's starting text.

Solution 
C, | F,3 A, C3 F, |]

Then think about the whole piece: 21 bars on two staves. What does an existing encoding save you, and what does it not?

docs.title: Two more ways in
docs.text:
Typing an encoding sign by sign is slow for a whole piece. There are two other ways to get the same five notes into the computer. Try one if you have time; the Any format box below the tabs shows the result of either.

A notation program: MuseScoreA language model

MuseScore is a free notation program: you enter notes with the mouse, the computer keyboard or a MIDI keyboard and see the score as you go, as in Sibelius, Finale or Dorico. It is not part of our setup; download it if you want to try.

  1. Create a score with one bass-clef staff (or a piano) in F major, 4/4, with an eighth-note pickup (how to make a pickup bar).
  2. Enter the five notes.
  3. Choose File → Export and save the score as MEI (MuseScore 4.2 or newer) or as uncompressed MusicXML (.musicxml) (exporting).
  4. Click Open a file in the box below and choose the exported file. It is read in your browser; nothing is uploaded.

A notation program is the quickest way to enter many notes. Once an edition has links to the scan and editorial notes, though, we edit its MEI directly: a round trip through a notation program can lose them.

A language model can turn notes written in words into an encoding. Write the notes the way you think of them, in English, in German or as letters, and ask for ABC or MEI. For example:

Write these notes in ABC notation and answer with the ABC only.
Schumann, Fröhlicher Landmann, left hand.
F major, common time, bass clef.
Pickup: C3 eighth.
Bar 1: F3 dotted quarter, A3 eighth, C4 dotted quarter, F3 eighth.

Use Copilot's chat in VS Code (setup, step 6) or any chat assistant in your browser. Paste the answer into the box below; it does not matter if the answer comes inside a code block. Then check it as in session 1: pitches and octaves, lengths, pickup, clef and key. Ask again for MEI instead of ABC, and compare.

The box finds out which format the text is in, draws the score and lists what Verovio reads. Show as MEI shows the same notes as MEI: that is how a result from MuseScore or a language model can become part of an MEI edition.

Extension: three more text formats

Part 2 of 02_note_entry.ipynb has the same five notes in Plaine & Easie, in MEI written by hand and in kern. You can paste each of them into the Any format box too. Compare your result with a neighbour who used another format.

docs.title: 6. The page and its bars
docs.text:
Continue 02_pdf_preparation.ipynb from the check where the setup stopped. The notebook

  1. downloads the scan and keeps it unchanged;
  2. copies page 8 into a one-page PDF (in that file it is page 1, but its printed number stays 8);
  3. draws the page as an image, which is what we link the bars to next session;
  4. lists which bars are on which system and checks that against the MEI file.

The print has no bar numbers, and the MEI file numbers the pickup as bar 1. To keep one vocabulary, we count bars as musicians do: the pickup is "the pickup", and bar 1 is the first full bar. This table connects the two numberings. The notebooks print the MEI number (n) and each bar's identifier (xml:id).

Bar MEI n System Bar's xml:id pickup 1 1 d1e9 1 2 1 d1e74 2 3 1 d1e352 3 4 1 d1e648 4 5 1 d1e968 5 6 2 d1e1231 6 7 2 d1e1509 7 8 2 d1e1805 8 9 2 d1e2125 9–12 10–13 3 13–16 14–17 4 17–20 18–21 5

Our edition covers the pickup and bars 1–8: the first two systems.

docs.title: 7. The note in the MEI file
docs.text:
Now find the wrong note from part 3 in the encoding. First in the score: here are the pickup and bar 1 of our starting file, with the F3 at the end of bar 1 selected. Click or tap any other note or rest, then come back to the F3.

Under the score you see the selected note three times: in words, as its line in the MEI file, and as the group of shapes that Verovio drew for it (notehead, stem, flag). The MEI line and the drawing carry the same identifier, here d1e338. That is how the drawing knows which note it shows. The pitch and the length, however, are only in the MEI file: the drawing only knows where to put its shapes.

What is SVG?

Verovio draws scores as SVG (Scalable Vector Graphics): a picture described as text, such as "a circle here, this big, in this colour". Because the picture is text, it stays sharp at any size, and a program can find one note in it by its identifier. The SVG introduction shows a circle written as text, the same note symbol enlarged as pixels and as SVG, and the pickup note as MEI and as SVG. We use SVG again next session, when we link the score to the scan.

Now find the same note in the file itself:

LaptopCloud
  1. In VS Code's file list on the left, open the folder schumann_edition_work next to the notebook, then inputs, then the one folder inside it (its name is a code, such as b02b5197b383), and click starter.mei. This is our starting file.
  2. Press Ctrl+F (macOS: Cmd+F) and type "d1e338", with the quotation marks.
  1. In JupyterLab's file browser, open work → camat_lectures → 02-building-an-edition → schumann_edition_work → inputs → the one folder inside it (its name is a code, such as b02b5197b383), and double-click starter.mei. This is our starting file; it opens as text.
  2. Choose Edit → Find…, type "d1e338", with the quotation marks, and click the arrow pointing down (Next Match) next to the search field.

You land on <note xml:id="d1e338" pname="f" oct="3" dur="8" .../>: the last bass note of bar 1, F3, an eighth. Scroll up to the <measure n="2" ...> it belongs to. Without the quotation marks, the search first finds the same ID in the file's header, where our correction is described.

Every note in the file has such an xml:id. It is how the drawing, the scan links and your corrections point at exactly this note, and how you can name it to a language model next session. HOMR's MusicXML and your ABC from part 5 have no such identifiers. Do not change the file yet: next session we edit a copy of it.

Extension: the same note in mei-friend

Open the MEI Sample Collection's file in mei-friend, the editor we use from session 3 on. Click Got it! if a welcome box appears. The link selects this note: it is blue in the score, and the code on the right shows its line. There it is still pname="a", the A3 from part 3.

Why does the starting file have no slurs or dynamics?

We removed the slurs, dynamics, tempo words and articulation from Maja Hartwig's file on purpose. Restoring some of them from the print is one of the editing tasks in session 3. The file's header says exactly what was removed.

docs.text:

  • 02_pdf_preparation.ipynb with schumann-edition-inputs.zip: parts 1 and 6. Downloads the scan from IMSLP when you run it. Next session continues in the folder schumann_edition_work that it creates.
  • 02_schumann_omr.ipynb with schumann-omr-recordings.zip: part 4.
  • 02_note_entry.ipynb: part 5. No ZIP needed.

docs.text:
• The print: Robert Schumann, Album für die Jugend, Op. 68, ed. Clara Schumann, Leipzig: Breitkopf & Härtel, plate R.S. 67 (IMSLP work page, file 51556; scan: Bayerische Staatsbibliothek). The notebooks download it when you run them; it is not part of the course files.
  • The encoding: Maja Hartwig, Fröhlicher Landmann, MEI 5.1, MEI Sample Collection. The file declares itself public domain; the collection is under the ECL-2.0 licence. Our starting file keeps its credits.
  • The full record of source and encoding: sources.json.
  • OMR programs: HOMR, OeMeR.
  • A finished facsimile-linked edition: Webern, Variations Op. 27.
